brief.what_broke: 12 session(s) waiting on locks. Root blocker(s): pid 129046 (batch_worker/batch_replayable_inventory, idle in transaction, txn open 61.8s) blocks 1 session(s); last statement: SELECT 1
brief.who_is_affected: Checkout success 25% over 30s (88/118 failed) vs SLO 95%. Revenue run-rate $18,400/min; about $13,722/min at risk. Verification window 10s. The business tolerates at most 60s of degraded checkout.

options.description: Terminate the root blocker session (batch_worker/batch_replayable_inventory, pid 129046) to release its locks.
Take no action; let the blocker finish and monitor checkout recovery.
options.cost: about $13,722/min of checkout revenue at risk while waiting

brief.recommendation: The root blocker batch_replayable_inventory (pid 129046) is may_interrupt and replayable (BIZ-2). Waiting costs ~$200,730 in lost checkout revenue over ~878s, which EXCEEDS the 60s degradation the business tolerates (BIZ-4, BIZ-7). Terminating incurs a 4-minute replay cost of inventory_reconcile (policy may_interrupt, BIZ-2), which is acceptable for a replayable workload. The business is losing ~$13,722/min at risk (BIZ-6), and the 60s tolerance window is already exceeded by the 22.3s blocker age plus the expected 878s remaining runtime.

audit.report: The batch_replayable_inventory workload stalled due to a root blocker (pid 129046) that had been idle in transaction for over 22 seconds. The Database Guardian recommended waiting, reasoning that the blocker remained under the 60-second business degradation window and that terminating would force a 4-minute replay of inventory_reconcile. The Continuity Guardian rejected every proposal, arguing that the cumulative revenue loss and waiting cost (~$200k) exceeded the 60-second tolerance, and that terminating was preferable for this may_interrupt, replayable workload. After three rounds with no agreement, the matter was escalated to the inventory-platform team.
audit.root_cause: A long-running batch transaction (batch_replayable_inventory) became the root blocker, holding locks that caused checkout degradation, but the guardians could not agree on whether to wait for natural completion or terminate and replay.
lessons: For may_interrupt, replayable workloads, pre‑calculate the replay cost (inventory_reconcile = 4 min) and the revenue‑at‑risk per minute ($13,722) so the trade-off can be resolved in the first round without iterative proposals.
audit.negotiation_critique: The Database Guardian consistently grounded proposals in the 60‑second tolerance and the 4‑minute replay cost, but repeatedly overlooked the change-calendar and protected‑settlements evidence the Continuity Guardian required. The Continuity Guardian rejected every wait proposal on the basis of exceeded degradation, yet did not provide the missing registry evidence to trigger the I3 consult‑owner path, causing a deadlock.
follow_ups: Add batch_replayable_inventory to the workload registry with its change-calendar window and protected‑settlements flag so future proposals can reference invariants I2/I3 immediately.
Publish the lock‑graph idle‑timer metric to the proposal UI so guardians see elapsed idle time before round 1.
Create a one‑page trade‑off sheet for may_interrupt, replayable workloads that lists the 4‑min replay cost and $13.7k/min revenue risk, to be attached to the first proposal.

The Continuity Guardian rejected every proposal, arguing that the cumulative revenue loss and waiting cost (~$200k) exceeded the 60-second tolerance, and that terminating was preferable for this may_interrupt, replayable workload. After three rounds with no agreement, the matter was escalated to the inventory-platform team.
audit.root_cause: A long-running batch transaction (batch_replayable_inventory) became the root blocker, holding locks that caused checkout degradation, but the guardians could not agree on whether to wait for natural completion or terminate and replay.
lessons: For may_interrupt, replayable workloads, pre‑calculate the replay cost (inventory_reconcile = 4 min) and the revenue‑at‑risk per minute ($13,722) so the trade-off can be resolved in the first round without iterative proposals.
audit.negotiation_critique: The Database Guardian consistently grounded proposals in the 60‑second tolerance and the 4‑minute replay cost, but repeatedly overlooked the change-calendar and protected‑settlements evidence the Continuity Guardian required. The Continuity Guardian rejected every wait proposal on the basis of exceeded degradation, yet did not provide the missing registry evidence to trigger the I3 consult‑owner path, causing a deadlock.
follow_ups: Add batch_replayable_inventory to the workload registry with its change-calendar window and protected‑settlements flag so future proposals can reference invariants I2/I3 immediately.
Publish the lock‑graph idle‑timer metric to the proposal UI so guardians see elapsed idle time before round 1.
Create a one‑page trade‑off sheet for may_interrupt, replayable workloads that lists the 4‑min replay cost and $13.7k/min revenue risk, to be attached to the first proposal.
